# Block 4: Extensions in action {.unnumbered} The base `ggplot2` grammar covers most chart types but makes several common visualisation tasks awkward. The extension packages below fill the gaps: - `ggdist` for distributional plots (raincloud, half-eye, point-interval); this is how you put *"show the raw data wherever sample size permits"* from Block 2 into practice. - `colorspace` and `colorBlindness` for palettes and accessibility checking; these put the encoding hierarchy and the accessibility principle from Block 1 into practice. - `ggrepel` and `ggtext` for direct labelling and rich text; these are the tools for the *direct labelling* and *highlighting* techniques in the audience table (Block 2). - `patchwork` for multi-panel composition, the natural alternative to `facet_wrap()` when subplots differ in chart type rather than data subset. Statistical annotation (significance brackets, p-value labels on figures) is not covered in this workshop. The principled approach is to fit a model with `emmeans` or equivalent and use `ggpubr::stat_pvalue_manual()` to render the contrasts. In a half-day workshop on visualisation principles, we leave statistical annotation to the wider statistical training in your programme. Each segment is short: a problem and a worked example to run along with the facilitator (the *In your own time* tasks are for after the session). Keep moving, because the block ends with a 🏆 **capstone challenge** where you race to recreate a published-style figure from scratch, on data you have not seen. There is a bonus after that: making a multi-panel figure interactive. ## Distributions with ggdist The default way to summarise a continuous variable across groups is a boxplot. A boxplot is informative but lossy: it shows quartiles and outliers but conceals the shape of the underlying distribution. Bimodality, skew, and gaps in the data all vanish. The **raincloud plot** (Allen et al., 2021) addresses this by combining three layers: a half-density (the "cloud") to show distribution shape, a slim boxplot for summary statistics, and jittered points (the "rain") for the raw data. `ggdist::stat_halfeye()` provides the cloud half. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins_complete |> ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species, colour = species)) + ggdist::stat_halfeye( adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.2, .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.8 ) + geom_boxplot( width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.4, colour = "grey20" ) + geom_jitter(width = 0.08, alpha = 0.4, size = 1.2) + colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") + colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "none", panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08d-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: Three things to notice. First, the cloud, the box, and the points are three separate layers stacked in a specific order: clouds at the back, box in the middle, points on top. Second, `justification = -0.2` shifts the cloud off the centre line so the box and points sit beside it rather than underneath. Third, the boxplot's outlier points are hidden with `outlier.shape = NA` because all the raw data are already shown as jittered points; leaving them on would double-count. ### In your own time :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Horizontal raincloud with point intervals :::: ::::{.task-container} Modify the worked example to flip the orientation (raincloud horizontal rather than vertical) and to use `ggdist::stat_pointinterval()` instead of the boxplot. `stat_pointinterval` shows the median and a range; work out from the documentation which range it shows by default. :::: :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins_complete |> ggplot(aes(y = species, x = body_mass_g, fill = species, colour = species)) + ggdist::stat_halfeye( adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.2, .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.8 ) + ggdist::stat_pointinterval( .width = c(0.5, 0.95), point_size = 2.5 ) + geom_jitter(height = 0.08, alpha = 0.2, size = 1.2, shape = 21) + colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") + colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") + labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = NULL) + theme_project(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` :::
## Accessible colour with colorspace and colorBlindness Two packages put the Block 1 principles into practice: `colorspace` builds the palette and `colorBlindness` checks it. Use them together, because a palette you have not checked leaves accessibility to chance. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fig <- penguins_complete |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm, colour = species, shape = species)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.8, size = 2) + colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") + labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Flipper length (mm)", colour = "Species", shape = "Species") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) # Inspect under simulated colour vision deficiency colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08d-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: The four-panel grid shows: the original, deuteranopia, protanopia, and a desaturated (greyscale) version. The figure passes if all groups remain distinguishable in all four panels. If any panel fails (typically deuteranopia or protanopia for red-green sensitive figures), strengthen the redundant encoding (shape or linetype), choose a more separated palette, or fall back to direct labelling. This is the encoding hierarchy from Block 1 in practice: position handles the two continuous variables (rank 1), colour hue handles the categorical (rank 2 for categorical data), and shape is added as a redundant cue so that the figure does not depend on colour alone. Shape is a weaker encoding on its own, but as a backup it is what keeps the groups apart in the greyscale panel. ### In your own time :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Redundant encoding under simulated CVD :::: ::::{.task-container} Build a scatter plot from `penguins_complete` using only `bill_length_mm` and `bill_depth_mm`, colour mapped to species, and *without* shape mapped redundantly. Run `colorBlindness::cvdPlot()`. Now add `shape = species` to the mapping and rerun. Compare the two outputs honestly. Which encoding survives the desaturation test? :::: :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Without redundant shape encoding fig_no_shape <- penguins_complete |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.8, size = 2) + colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") + theme_project(base_size = 12) colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig_no_shape) # With redundant shape encoding fig_with_shape <- fig_no_shape + aes(shape = species) + labs(colour = "Species", shape = "Species") colorBlindness::cvdPlot(fig_with_shape) ``` ::: The figure with redundant shape encoding survives the desaturated panel because the shape carries the species information when the colour information collapses. The figure without redundant encoding becomes unreadable in greyscale.
## Direct labelling with ggrepel and ggtext A figure legend separates the colour key from the data: the reader's eye has to travel from the data layer to the legend and back, holding a mapping in working memory. **Direct labelling** puts the group name on the data itself, so the eye reads the label as part of the data. For talks, posters, and public engagement, direct labelling is almost always clearer. The problem is that labels placed at data points overlap each other. `ggrepel::geom_text_repel()` and `ggrepel::geom_label_repel()` solve this by moving labels iteratively until they no longer collide, with connector lines preserved. The example below uses `geom_label_repel()`, which draws each label on a small background box. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Label location: one label per species at the species centroid label_data <- penguins_complete |> group_by(species) |> summarise(x = median(bill_length_mm), y = median(flipper_length_mm), .groups = "drop") penguins_complete |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm, colour = species)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) + ggrepel::geom_label_repel( data = label_data, aes(x = x, y = y, label = species, colour = species), size = 5, fontface = "bold", label.size = 0, inherit.aes = FALSE ) + colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") + labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Flipper length (mm)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08d-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: `ggtext` is the companion package for **rich text**: it allows markdown formatting inside titles, axis labels, and legend entries, and supports inline colour. This is what lets you write a title like `"**Gentoo** penguins are **substantially heavier** than Adelie and Chinstrap"` directly. To enable rich text on a theme element, set it to `ggtext::element_markdown()`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins_complete |> ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) + ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.2, .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.8) + geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5, colour = "grey20") + colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") + labs( title = "**Gentoo** penguins are substantially heavier than **Adelie** and **Chinstrap**", x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)" ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "none", plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 13, lineheight = 1.2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08d-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: Inline colour in the title removes the need for a separate legend entirely. The hex codes in the title are the three `Dark2` colours used for the fills (`colorspace::qualitative_hcl(3, palette = "Dark2")` returns them), so the colours in the title match the fills in the data, and the reader makes the mapping in a single saccade. These techniques put the *direct labelling* and *highlighting* rows of the audience table from Block 2 into practice. Reach for direct labels and inline-coloured titles when designing for posters, talks, or public engagement, where the reader cannot afford the eye-travel to a separate legend. ### In your own time :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Highlight one species in a rich-text title :::: ::::{.task-container} Take the rich-text title in the worked example and modify it so that only **Gentoo** is highlighted in colour (in `#5F96C2`, its `Dark2` fill), and the other two species names appear in plain text. Then add a subtitle that gives the sample sizes for each species. The subtitle should also be rich text, so you will need to set `plot.subtitle = ggtext::element_markdown()` in `theme()`. :::: :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n_species <- count(penguins_complete, species) penguins_complete |> ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) + ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.2, .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.8) + geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5, colour = "grey20") + colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") + labs( title = "**Gentoo** penguins are substantially heavier than Adelie and Chinstrap", subtitle = paste0("*Pygoscelis* spp., Palmer Archipelago (n = ", paste(n_species$n, n_species$species, collapse = ", "), ")"), x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)" ) + theme_project(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "none", plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 13, lineheight = 1.2), plot.subtitle = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 10, colour = "grey40")) ``` :::
## Multi-panel composition with patchwork For panels showing the same chart type for different subsets of the data, use `facet_wrap()` or `facet_grid()`. For panels showing different chart types or different aspects of one analysis, use `patchwork`. Three defaults apply for `patchwork` compositions: collect legends into a single shared legend, tag panels with uppercase letters, and use an explicit `design = ` string for the layout. The string is self-documenting; you can rearrange the layout by editing the letters without rewriting the composition call. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pal <- colorspace::qualitative_hcl(3, palette = "Dark2") names(pal) <- levels(penguins_complete$species) p1 <- penguins_complete |> ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) + ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.2, .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.8) + geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) + scale_fill_manual(values = pal, name = "Species") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + guides(fill = "none") p2 <- penguins_complete |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, fill = species, shape = species)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7) + scale_fill_manual(values = pal, name = "Species") + scale_shape_manual(values = c(21,22,23), name = "Species") + labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) p3 <- penguins_complete |> count(species, island) |> ggplot(aes(x = island, y = n, fill = species)) + geom_col(position = position_dodge2(preserve = "single")) + scale_fill_manual(values = pal, name = "Species") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Count") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + guides(fill = "none") # Edit the letter grid below to rearrange panels. # Letters refer to plots in the order they are added (A = p1, B = p2, C = p3). layout <- " AB CC " p1 + p2 + p3 + patchwork::plot_layout(design = layout, guides = "collect") + patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") & theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08d-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse = "true"} ## guides When you combine plots with patchwork and set `guides = "collect"`, patchwork gathers legends from every panel and merges any it considers identical. "Identical" is strict: the guides must share the same aesthetic, scale, breaks and title. If your panels encode the same grouping variable through different aesthetics (say fill in one panel and colour plus shape in another) or through different scales, patchwork treats them as distinct and shows one legend per panel rather than a single shared key. - First, decide which single legend should represent the shared variable across all panels, and choose the panel whose legend carries the most visual encoding, since that legend can serve as a complete key for the others. - Second, suppress the legends on the remaining panels with `guides( = "none")`. Without step two you get this. The three panels below use different aesthetics and scales and none of them suppresses its legend, so patchwork collects three separate legends: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} q1 <- penguins_complete |> ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) + ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.2, .width = 0, point_colour = NA, alpha = 0.8) + geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.5) + colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) q2 <- penguins_complete |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = species, shape = species)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7) + colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") + labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) q3 <- penguins_complete |> count(species, island) |> ggplot(aes(x = species, y = n, fill = island)) + geom_col(position = "dodge") + colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Set 2") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Count") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) # Edit the letter grid below to rearrange panels. # Letters refer to plots in the order they are added (A = q1, B = q2, C = q3). layout <- " AB CC " q1 + q2 + q3 + patchwork::plot_layout(design = layout, guides = "collect") + patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") & theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08d-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: The `&` operator applies its right-hand side to every subplot already in the composition, so use it for global theme settings like legend position and tag formatting. The `+` operator applies only to the most recently added subplot. :::{.callout-tip} **Try later.** Change the layout string so that panels A and C are stacked on the left and panel B occupies the full right column (`"AB\nCB\n"`). ::: Use multi-panel composition for figures that combine several aspects of one analysis into a single figure. A typical journal "Figure 1" with three panels labelled A, B, C is almost always a `patchwork` composition, not a `facet_wrap()`. The layout string makes the composition easy to edit: if a reviewer asks you to rearrange the panels, you change the letters rather than rewrite the code. ### In your own time :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Rearrange the patchwork layout :::: ::::{.task-container} Take the three-panel composition from the worked example. Change the `layout` string so that panel A spans the entire top row, and panels B and C share the bottom row. Then change `tag_levels = "A"` to `tag_levels = "i"` (lowercase Roman numerals) and observe the change. Finally, change `tag_levels` to `c("A", "i")` for nested tagging and see what happens. :::: :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} layout <- " AA BC " p1 + p2 + p3 + patchwork::plot_layout(design = layout, guides = "collect") + patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") & theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)) # With lowercase Roman numeral tags p1 + p2 + p3 + patchwork::plot_layout(design = layout, guides = "collect") + patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "i") & theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)) # Nested tagging is for compositions of compositions; with a single # layer of subplots, c("A", "i") behaves the same as "A". ``` :::
## 🏆 Capstone challenge: recreate this figure Time to put the whole block together on data you have not seen. `CO2` is built into R: CO~2~ uptake by 12 grass plants from **Quebec** and **Mississippi**, half of them chilled overnight, each measured at seven CO~2~ concentrations. Here is your target: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08d-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Recreate the figure: how far can you get? (solo race, 15 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} Everyone starts at Bronze. Post 🥉, 🥈 or 🥇 in the chat each time you clear a tier. The first Gold screenshot wins. Stuck? Post your error message in the chat; anyone who helps fix it gets a shout-out. - 🥉 **Bronze: panel B.** Raw points for each Treatment, dodged by Type, with a median bar, in the two Type colours. *Hint:* `position_jitterdodge()` and `stat_summary(geom = "crossbar")`. - 🥈 **Silver: panel A.** One line per plant, colour by Type, linetype by Treatment, and **direct labels** instead of a colour legend. *Hint:* `group = Plant`, and `ggrepel` on a small data frame of line ends. - 🥇 **Gold: the full figure.** Both panels side by side (A twice as wide), tagged A and B, with the coloured rich-text title and proper sub/superscripts in the axis titles. *Hint:* `patchwork`, `plot_annotation()` and `ggtext::element_markdown()`. :::: :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} co2_pal <- c(Quebec = "#1B9E77", Mississippi = "#D95F02") CO2 |> ggplot(aes(Treatment, uptake, colour = Type)) + geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.6), alpha = 0.6) + stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.25, position = position_dodge(0.6), linewidth = 0.4) + scale_colour_manual(values = co2_pal) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) ``` :::
The full code for the target figure. Silver is `target_a`; Gold adds the composition at the end. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} co2_ends <- CO2 |> filter(conc == max(conc)) |> summarise(uptake = mean(uptake), .by = Type) |> mutate(conc = 1000) target_a <- CO2 |> ggplot(aes(conc, uptake, colour = Type, group = Plant, linetype = Treatment)) + geom_line(alpha = 0.7) + geom_point(size = 1.2) + ggrepel::geom_text_repel( data = co2_ends, aes(conc, uptake, label = Type, colour = Type), inherit.aes = FALSE, nudge_x = 80, direction = "y", hjust = 0, fontface = "bold", segment.colour = NA) + scale_colour_manual(values = co2_pal, guide = "none") + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1250), breaks = seq(0, 1000, 250)) + labs(x = "Ambient CO2 (mL L-1)", y = "CO2 uptake (µmol m-2 s-1)", linetype = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(), axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown(), legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) target_b <- CO2 |> ggplot(aes(Treatment, uptake, colour = Type)) + geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.6), alpha = 0.6) + stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.25, position = position_dodge(0.6), linewidth = 0.4) + scale_colour_manual(values = co2_pal, guide = "none") + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) (target_a + target_b + plot_layout(widths = c(2, 1))) + plot_annotation( tag_levels = "A", title = "Chilling cuts CO2 uptake in **Mississippi** grasses far more than in **Quebec** ones", theme = theme(plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 13))) ``` :::
## Bonus: linked, interactive panels with ggiraph Block 2 introduced `ggiraph` for a single plot. It also works on a whole `patchwork` composition, and that is where it gets fun: give every panel the same `data_id`, and hovering in *one* panel highlights the same group in *all* of them. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggiraph) i1 <- penguins_complete |> ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, colour = species, data_id = species, tooltip = paste0(species, ": ", body_mass_g, " g"))) + geom_jitter_interactive(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.6) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)") i2 <- penguins_complete |> ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = species, data_id = species, tooltip = paste0(species, ": ", bill_length_mm, " × ", bill_depth_mm, " mm"))) + geom_point_interactive(alpha = 0.7) + labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)") i3 <- penguins_complete |> count(species, island) |> ggplot(aes(x = island, y = n, fill = species, data_id = species, tooltip = paste0(species, " on ", island, ": ", n))) + geom_col_interactive(position = position_dodge2(preserve = "single")) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Count") linked <- (i1 + i2) / i3 & colorspace::scale_fill_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") & colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark2") & theme_minimal(base_size = 11) & theme(legend.position = "none") girafe(ggobj = linked, width_svg = 8, height_svg = 6, options = list(opts_hover(css = "stroke:black;stroke-width:1.5px;"), opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.15;"))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Hover over any Gentoo point or bar and watch the other two panels follow. (Panel A is a strip of raw points rather than a boxplot: `geom_boxplot_interactive()` tags each box by its group *number*, not its species, so it would not link up.) The recipe is the same one you already know: interactive geoms, a shared `data_id`, then `girafe()`. Everything else (the `patchwork` layout, `&` for shared settings, the `Dark2` palette) is unchanged from the static version. :::{.callout-tip} **Try later.** Add `opts_selection(type = "single")` to the `options` list and click a group instead of hovering. Then save the figure for a lab website with `htmlwidgets::saveWidget(girafe(ggobj = linked), "linked_penguins.html")`. :::
